The Equilibrium of the Ego

Classical lessons on winning and losing

Achilles and Ajax playing a board game, c. 510 BCE.
Credit: Medea Group, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

I don’t usually pick up an old book to learn a lesson about human nature; I’m usually just looking for some uncanny humor, or testing the claim—albeit subjectively—that old books are inherently richer than new ones. But that might change from now on. The shift comes down to some recent thoughts I’ve had while spending time with Sophocles’ tragedy, Ajax, and Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey. For how old and far away the characters in these books are, I’m tempted to think I and humanity have progressed past the struggles and problems they faced; but I’ve realized the character flaws and arrogance of Ancient Greece are the same as in modern times.

Let’s take Ajax in Sophocles’ tragedy. He is unarguably the next best elite military commander after Achilles himself according to the poems. In the Iliad, Homer describes him as a literal fortress of a man, the “wall of the Achaeans,” who single-handedly held off entire Trojan regiments to protect the Greek ships. So when Achilles died and his armor was up for grabs, Ajax naturally expected to receive it. But when his competitor Odysseus outmaneuvered him by delivering a convincing speech that persuaded the Greek generals to award him the prize, Ajax harbored a bitter grudge towards Odysseus—his long-time companion in the Trojan war—that persisted even into the afterlife, where the Poet tells us Ajax’s ghost still refuses to speak to him. Moreover, that grudge drove him to immediate self-sabotage. In a fit of rage, he lashed out at grazing sheep, slaughtering them in the dark under the delusion that they were the political rivals who chose Odysseus, before ultimately destroying himself. It was a humiliatingly pathetic end for a legendary general whom Homer once exalted as second only to Achilles in grade and power. So, how can a loss sow this level of resentment towards a once-loyal comrade and trusted friend, and blind a hero into such a tragic end? In the elite world of Homeric warfare, Ajax read that loss as a verdict on his inherent worth as a soldier. After all, this is Achilles’ armor—the paragon of military strength—and it had been awarded to someone else, based on anything but military strength. The main reason, from my perspective, why someone would refuse to accept the loss and see that the standard for winning had changed is a brittle ego. Ajax attached his entire identity to that armor and couldn’t see himself living in a world where physical strength was not the ultimate standard for military assessment. For me, this is sobering. While my identity isn’t fixated on Achilles’ armor, I can certainly think of situations where the temptation to let an external prize define my worth has almost brought with it a similar self-destruction.

But if Ajax’s demise illustrates how not to handle a loss, Odysseus’ journey back to Ithaca after the Trojan War offers a masterclass in how not to handle a win. Trapped in the cave of the Cyclops Polyphemus on his return trip, Odysseus executes a brilliant tactical move that allows him to save himself and the remaining members of his crew who hadn’t already been eaten.

By calling himself “Nobody”, he prevents Polyphemus from successfully rallying his fellow Cyclopes for help; when the giant cries out in agony after being blinded, he can only scream that “Nobody” is ruining him. This clever ruse allows the remaining crew members to slip out of the cave undetected, strapped to the bellies of the Cyclops’ sheep. However, on his way out, once safely on his ship, Odysseus is overcome by a fit of arrogance. He wants to make absolutely sure that Polyphemus knows exactly who defeated him. So he screams his true name across the water to the shore.

That single victory lap ruined everything. Armed with Odysseus’ actual identity, Polyphemus invokes a devastating curse from his father, Poseidon, that keeps Odysseus trapped at sea for ten additional years—costing him the lives of his entire crew. He finally returns to Ithaca, but at what cost? And all because he had to make sure he was known for this win. For a man known as one of the most clever tacticians in epic poetry, this blunder is almost impossible to explain. In that moment, blinded by the need for recognition, he forgot about everything that actually mattered: his wife Penelope, who would wait another decade for him; his son Telemachus, who grew up without a father; and the very friends journeying by his side. The man who could defeat a Cyclops with pure wit lacked the basic self-control to sail away quietly. It forces a challenging moment of self-reflection about how to win well, especially in a culture where we focus almost entirely on the end result rather than the hidden costs of how we get there.

So naturally, I had to ask: did these guys just not know the cost of unbridled arrogance?

I highly doubt it. In the Iliad, when the Greeks are being severely beaten down because Achilles begged his mother to have Zeus turn the tide of the war, Agamemnon sends an embassy to plead with him. The delegation includes Ajax, Odysseus, and Phoenix—Achilles’ own childhood mentor. Both Ajax and Odysseus sat right there in the tent and heard Phoenix’s heartbreaking speech warning Achilles about how bitter, unyielding pride inevitably destroys a man and everything he loves. They watched Achilles harden his heart even after Agamemnon publicly recanted and offered to vindicate him, a stubbornness that ultimately set the stage for his closest companion, Patroclus, to die. They were no strangers to self-destruction. Yet, when their own moments came, they repeated the script. That tells me that simply possessing knowledge about a flaw doesn’t mean we won’t succumb to it when our own pride is tested. So, what would it have taken for these two men to just chill? It is easy for me to look from the outside and say, “Well, I should just learn from this and be more alert to my own arrogance.” But fundamentally, if even Odysseus—the most calculating and careful man in epic poetry—succumbed to a victory lap, and if Ajax couldn’t absorb the wisdom of the camp’s greatest mentors, can I really say that I will easily move past the temptation the next time a major loss or win comes my way? Maybe I will, and maybe I won’t. But if there is one thing I have learned from spending time with these ancient texts, it’s that we haven’t actually evolved past our psychological blind spots. For all our progress as a species, our internal wiring remains exactly the same.
